prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The monocular depth map depicts the enclosed interior and doorway of a small camping tent, showing bright foreground bedding and tent flaps within arm's reach (roughly 0.3–0.8 m away) and a darker back tent wall about 1.5–2.0 m in front of the camera wearer. Across the five frames, it tracks a person in a cap on the right side (about 1.0–1.5 m away in frames 2 and 4, facing left in profile and looking down toward the bedding rather than at the camera wearer) alongside bundles of red and blue sleeping bags or blankets and pillows resting on the tent floor below eye level, spaced 0.3–0.6 m from each other. As the camera wearer shifts position and turns slightly left and right across the sequence, the bright left tent doorway flap and foreground bedding move closer and further, culminating in frame 5 where a translucent mesh screen hangs directly in front of the lens (0.2–0.4 m away) and partially occludes the bedding behind it. This map makes it much easier than the motion-blurred RGB frames to distinguish the 3D layering between the overhanging tent entrance flap, the foreground sleeping bags, and the recessed back wall. However, the depth map is unreliable in frame 5 where it renders the see-through mesh panel as an opaque solid wall, and in frames 1 and 4 where smooth, low-texture tent walls appear excessively dark as if at infinite distance.
descriptions.segmentation: The instance segmentation map isolates specific regions within the tent scene, correctly outlining the person on the right edge of frames 2 and 4 (roughly 1.0–1.5 m away, facing left and partly cropped by the right frame border, within arm's reach of the blue pillow and red bedding below them). Across the five frames, as the camera wearer turns and moves near the tent entrance, the person enters view on the right in frame 2, disappears off the right edge in frame 3, reappears more upright in frame 4, and is gone or occluded in frame 5 as the camera shifts left toward the mesh flap. While the mask in frames 2 and 4 provides a sharper silhouette of the dark-clothed person against the dark tent floor than the dim RGB image alone, the segmentation map is largely unreliable across the rest of the strip. It completely misses the person's edge in frame 1 and misclassifies the foreground bedding and pillows (0.3–1.2 m away) as a single 'person' mask, mislabels the tent walls (1.0–2.0 m away) and red sleeping bag (0.5–1.0 m away) as 'umbrella' in frame 3, and misidentifies the close-up mesh screen and bedding (0.2–0.8 m away) as 'potted plant' in frame 5.
descriptions.pose: The body and hand skeleton map is completely blank (entirely black) across all five frames, failing to detect any body or hand keypoints in the scene. In the RGB strip, a person wearing a cap and dark jacket is present on the right side of the tent interior at roughly 1.0–1.5 m distance in frames 2 and 4 (and barely visible at the top-right edge in frame 1 and right edge in frame 3), leaning forward in frame 2 and sitting more upright in frame 4 while facing left away from the camera wearer and within arm's reach of the pillows and blankets below. Because the person is heavily occluded by the right edge of the frame, wears dark clothing that blends into the shadowed tent floor, and has their hands hidden beneath or behind the bedding, the pose estimator fails to register any skeletal structure. Consequently, this map provides no spatial information that is hard to see in the RGB alone and is completely unreliable for tracking the person's posture, orientation, or hand positions across the sequence.
